description_full: Ecopetrol S.A. operates as an integrated energy company. It operates through four segments: Exploration and Production; Transport and Logistics; Refining and Petrochemicals; and Energy transmission and Toll Roads Concessions. The Exploration and Production segment engages in the exploration and production of oil and gas. The Transport and Logistics segment is involved in the transportation of crude oil, motor fuels, fuel oil, and other refined products, including diesel, jet, and biofuels. The Refining and Petrochemicals segment refines and processes crude oil at the Barrancabermeja and Cartagena refineries; and distributes natural gas and LPG. The energy Transmission and Toll Roads Concessions segment supplies transmission and information technology and telecommunications services, as well as designs, develops, constructs, operates, and maintains road and energy infrastructure projects. The company operates in Colombia, the United States, China, Brazil, India, Singapore and other Asian countries, Peru, Chile, Other South America countries, Central America and the Caribbean, and Europe. The company was formerly known as Empresa Colombiana de Petróleos and changed its name to Ecopetrol S.A. in June 2003. Ecopetrol S.A. was incorporated in 1948 and is based in Bogotá, Colombia.
financial_summary: Ecopetrol S.A. is a large-cap energy business with a $31.7B market cap on $32.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 8% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 38%.

The business throws off $8.8B in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.44× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.7×.

Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 13% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Trading at a 70% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk
Energy sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter
Energy ETF in a sustained uptrend above its long-term average

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 13pp above the Energy median (16%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.65x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.8% of sector revenue and 2.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 84% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 0.56, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.24 vs 5y 0.33), so read it loosely.
About $25.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 68% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 44% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 70% below its DCF fair value of $50.91, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 3%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $39.30 to $66.41 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 8.2 vs 13.6 and P/FCF 3.6 vs 14.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 77% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 27.7% (above the risk-free rate).
The 11 covering analysts target $15.53 on average, 1% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.38).
It runs a 38% gross margin and converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.44x.
ROE of 25% is amplified by 3.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($3.4B of cash against $27.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.52 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.1% over 3 years and 8.5% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 38%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 21.3% on average.
Analysts expect -21.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 1%.
It returns 4.2% a year to shareholders (4.2% in dividends).
